title: Engineering Vacuum Fluctuations in Hyperbolic Heterostructures
authors: Jie-Cheng Feng, Xinle Cheng, Itai Keren, Dante M. Kennes, Abhay N. Pasupathy, Dmitri N. Basov, Emil Vinas Bostrom, Angel Rubio
abstract: Vacuum fluctuations can be engineered using optical cavities, resonators, and surface-polaritonic modes, but extending such control deep inside a material remains challenging.Here we show that the vacuum field inside a hyperbolic material can be reshaped by a much thinner overlayer with opposite hyperbolicity.This effect requires overlap between the hyperbolic bands of the two materials and modifies the coupling between the vacuum field and matter excitations within the bottom material, without changing its intrinsic dielectric properties. As an application, we use Eliashberg theory to study a two-dimensional superconducting layer inside the bottom material, showing that the overlayer can remotely change its critical temperature.Our results may shed light on recent experiments reporting changes in superconductivity arising from a frequency-matched hyperbolic overlayer, and suggest an on-chip route to long-range control of matter excitations and collective material properties.
summary: This paper proposes using hyperbolic heterostructures to actively engineer the vacuum electromagnetic field deep within a material. By placing a thin overlayer, researchers can reshape the vacuum fluctuations, which is then shown to remotely tune the superconducting critical temperature of an embedded 2D layer. This suggests a novel, on-chip route for controlling quantum material properties via vacuum field engineering.
main_problem: The challenge is to engineer and control the quantum vacuum fluctuations deep inside a material structure, moving beyond surface-level control.
main_result: A thin overlayer with opposite hyperbolicity can remotely reshape the vacuum field inside a hyperbolic material, which in turn can modify the critical temperature of an embedded superconductor.
method: The study uses theoretical modeling involving the hybridization of hyperbolic polariton modes and applies Eliashberg theory to analyze the superconducting response.
model_or_system: The system is a hyperbolic heterostructure composed of a bottom hyperbolic material (HMb) and a thin overlayer (HMt). The physics is governed by the coupling between the vacuum field and matter excitations, such as phonons or superconducting pairs.
key_observables: Vacuum fluctuations of the in-plane electric field ($\langle E_{2x} angle_{vac}$) and the superconducting critical temperature ($T_c$).
important_parameters: The degree of overlap between the hyperbolic bands of the two materials, and the thickness of the overlayer.
main_assumptions: The analysis simplifies quantization by neglecting the damping term, and the model is not intended as a quantitative description of specific experiments.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the directional control of vacuum fluctuations, showing enhancement of the in-plane field when capped by HMt, and demonstrate that $T_c$ changes only when the hyperbolic bands overlap.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of vacuum control, models the hyperbolic heterostructure, calculates the field modification via mode hybridization, and applies this control mechanism to predict changes in superconductivity using Eliashberg theory.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering of vacuum fields in structured media, which is a key area in quantum optics and open quantum systems, providing a mechanism for long-range, non-local control over material properties.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Directional control of vacuum fluctuations in a hyperbolic phonon polariton heterostructure. Left: In a bare hyperbolic material HMb, the relevant phonon- polariton mode is dominated by a material excitation with out-of-plane polarization, such that the vacuum fluctuations of the in-plane electric field ⟨E2 x⟩vac are weak. Right: HMb is capped by a second hyperbolic material HMt, with differ- ently oriented anisotropy arising from a material excitation with primarily in-plane polarization. When the hyperbolic frequency windows overlap, the polariton modes hybridize and enhance ⟨E2 x⟩vac deep inside HMb.
